examples.problem: The half-life of bismuth-210 is $5.012$ days. How long does it take for a $1\,280\,\textrm g$ sample of bismuth-210 to reduce to $5\,\textrm g?$
examples.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that $t_{1/2} = 5.012$ days we have

$$
5.012 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{5.012}
$$

Also, since $M_0 = 1\,280\,\textrm g,$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t) = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
5 = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =1\,280{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{5}{1\,280} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{1}{256} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{256}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ t & =\frac{5.012\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡256}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{5\,\text{g}}{1\,280\,\text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{256} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{8},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t) =  \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^8\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $8$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $1\,280\,\textrm g$ to $5\,\textrm g.$ Hence,

$$
t = 8\cdot t_{1/2} =8 \cdot 5.012 \approx 40.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$

feedback.problem:
The mass $M(t),$ in micrograms, of a sample of rhodium-101 is given by

$$
M(t)=7{e}^{-0.21t},
$$

where $t$ is the time, in years. Rounded to one decimal place, what is the half-life of rhodium-101?
feedback.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

We're given that $k=0.21.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1/2} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{0.21} \\  & ≈3.3\,\text{years}.\end{aligned}
$$
